note: Source archives remain verbatim. This file curates the active graph. Sources support content scopes; edge strengths and directions are editorial inferences.

merges.reason: Both records locate ordered pairs in all four quadrants; different upstream age labels do not create a new skill.
Both cover coordinate translations, reflections and rotations preserving lengths and angles.
Both describe and perform reflections and translations on a grid; retain this narrower skill separately from rotations.
Both interpret probability on the same zero-to-one scale.
Both cover exhaustive probability totals and P(not A)=1-P(A); retain both objectives in the combined profile.
Both explain equivalent fractions by repartitioning visual models of an unchanged whole.
Both cover full-turn, straight-line and opposite-angle facts; retain opposite angles explicitly.
Both express and simplify multiplicative ratios; preserve part-to-part versus part-to-whole interpretation.
Both locate unit and non-unit fractions by equal subdivision of a number line; the later record adds examples of the same method.
Both construct and critique multi-step mathematical arguments. Different arithmetic examples do not warrant a serial prerequisite between copies of the same general reasoning skill.
Both scale decimal numbers by 10, 100 and 1000 using place value, and their examples overlap. Retain the full method without the inconsistent three-decimal-place cap in the later description.

topic_patches.name: Total probability and complementary events
topic_patches.description: Probabilities of mutually exclusive outcomes covering every possibility sum to one. An event and its complement form such a partition, so P(not A)=1−P(A).
learning_objectives: Check that an exhaustive probability table has non-negative probabilities summing to one.
Calculate a complementary probability without recounting all outcomes.

questions.question: A spinner has exactly three possible colours with model probabilities 0.2, 0.3 and 0.4. Can this be its complete probability table?
questions.answer: No; the probabilities total 0.9, so 0.1 is unaccounted for.
questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive outcomes covering every possibility must have probabilities summing to one.
hints: Compare the sum with the probability of any outcome occurring.

applicability.notes: Editorial diagnostic; use the linked curriculum scope and check the learner’s number representations before choosing it. This does not establish an assessment grade.

questions.question: Two straight lines cross. One angle is 117°. What are the vertically opposite angle and an adjacent angle?
questions.answer: The opposite angle is 117°; an adjacent angle is 63°.
questions.explanation: Opposite angles are equal. Adjacent angles on a straight line total 180°.
hints: Identify the angle across the crossing.
Use the straight line to find the neighbouring angle.

questions.question: There are 2 red beads for every 3 blue beads. What fraction of the blue count is the red count, and what fraction of all beads is red?
questions.answer: The red count is 2/3 of the blue count; 2/5 of all beads are red.
questions.explanation: The comparison denominator is three blue parts in the first question and five total parts in the second.
hints: Name the quantity being compared with red in each question.
Draw two red parts and three blue parts.

questions.question: On a probability scale from 0 to 1, where do impossible, an even chance and certain belong?
questions.explanation: The endpoints represent impossible and certain; an even chance sits halfway between them.
